- the Senja team

reader_verdicts.relevance_feedback: Profile-supported: I run cohort-based courses and need student video on camera before the next launch, and collecting feedback for course marketing is something I do. The email speaks straight to that — forcing video rather than hoping for it, and treating a cohort as a list, matches how I'd actually have to do this. Email-only presuppositions: that I have my last cohort's addresses in a mailing list or a CSV (plausible, but nowhere established), that reminders and non-responders are my current bottleneck, and that I don't already have a way of doing this. Unknowns: what I currently use (nothing established), whether my hesitation is logistics or the asking itself, and what happens to the video once collected — the email never says whether I can put it on a sales page, which is the only reason I want it. Timing: the profile gives me a launch ahead, not a date; the email wisely doesn't invent one.

brief.interpretation: Read literally: one cold acquisition email, in English, to the selected course-creator segment, ending at the documented self-serve free signup. First contact, not onboarding — the reader has no account, so the email earns one small first action rather than activating a feature. Three narrowings carried over, plus one repair. (1) The current dossier qualifies the segment to cohort-based course operators (RECOMMENDED_NARROW), so the argument stays inside that slice. (2) The segment name says "needs student results on camera before the next cohort launch", but verified research explicitly does not establish an imminent launch, a video-only need, or any installed course platform, so none of those may be asserted. (3) The strategy remains the asking mechanism — a structured invite plus a bounded follow-up schedule — because that is the documented part of the researched problem that works with no paid plan and no connected platform, and the documented next action remains the offer sheet's "Sign up for free" to https://app.senja.io/signup. The repair: the previous version's promise ("the praise a cohort already gives you can become publishable testimonials") smuggled a response claim into the premise, and P3 was attached as a second problem, which pulled the argument toward "ask at the right time and you get stronger testimonials". Neither is established. This version drops P3 from the premise, keeps only P1's grounded reluctance, and states the claim strictly as the reader's own control: what they configure once, and how small the thing they are asking a student for is. Nothing in the primary argument now asserts, implies or hints at a reply, a rate, or the quality of what comes back. A complete alternative proposition is included — the shape of the ask and the consent choice, ending on the official read-only form-setup page, which is the right first ask for a cold reader whose question is whether the form can ask what they need at all.

brief.promise: Asking a cohort for testimonials can be something you set up once — one form, one invite list, reminders capped at three and aimed only at the students who have not answered — instead of a decision you re-make, student by student, every few days.
brief.orientation: For a small course or coaching team collecting student feedback for course and cohort sales pages, Senja is a tool for requesting text or video testimonials and displaying or reusing the responses.
brief.arc: One email, one move. Open on the part of the job that actually stalls — not the first ask but the second one, and the nerve it takes to send it. Show the mechanism that turns the chasing into a setting. Hand over the student-side cost so the size of the request is concrete rather than imagined. Close on a free signup with one invite as the test. Because it stands alone, nothing is deferred: the mechanism, its bounds and the next step all appear here, and the email claims nothing about what comes back.
brief.sequence_rationale: One email was requested in so many words, so the whole argument fits a single read. Angle choice, unchanged and still deliberate: (a) the course-platform trigger (E49/E48) is the seductive wrong lead — paid plan, connected platform, and the only evidence of platform use is one creator's 2022 retrospective; (b) display and reuse (E99, E24, E103, E159) argues about the destination to a reader with nothing to display yet; (c) price is the biggest shelf by count and wins arguments for a vendor-comparing reader, which this one is not. The invite mechanism is the only angle that is LEAD-ranked, dossier-linked to a verified problem, and usable on a free account with no prerequisite. What this repair changes: the premise now carries P1 only. P3 was dropped, because its own grounding is a creator's claim that prompt asking produces stronger testimonials — a quality-of-response claim the selected evidence does not establish — and keeping it in the brief invited exactly the drift the defect names. With P1 alone, every field describes something the reader controls: who gets invited, whether reminders are on, how many there are and when, and what a student is asked to do. Objection: P1's reluctance ("I don't want to seem pushy") is grounded, applies directly to the requested step, and has a real documented answer — follow-ups are optional, capped at three, on a fixed 1/3/7-day schedule, and reach only non-responders, while the student side is a page with no account and no software that Senja describes as about thirty seconds. Deliberately left unanswerable and therefore kept off the page: how students react to reminders, what share of a cohort replies, and whether what arrives is good enough to publish. The alternative proposition is a different bet — the shape of the ask and the consent choice rather than reach and persistence — and it ends on the official support page that documents it, so a cold reader can settle whether the form can ask what they need before creating anything.

The invite mechanism is LEAD-ranked evidence (E151) that the current dossier links to P1, it is the one documented way to ask and then ask again that needs no paid plan and no connected course platform, and the free self-serve signup is the documented action that lets them configure it on a real cohort. It is also the only angle whose entire payoff sits on the creator's side of the exchange, which is the only side the evidence covers.
emails.argument_issue: The licensed evidence establishes what the creator can configure — who is invited, whether reminders run, how many and when — and what the student is asked to do. It establishes nothing about response: not rate, not reception, not the quality or usability of what arrives. Every field here is written on the creator's side of that line, and the copy has to stay there: control over the ask and the documented size of the request, never the reply.
emails.job: Get a cohort course operator to create a free account, build one invite to a recent cohort, and switch on the follow-up schedule before sending it.
emails.single_idea: The ask that never goes out is the second one — and that one does not need nerve, it needs a setting: at most three reminders, 1, 3 and 7 days after the invite, only to the students who have not answered.
emails.felt_need: A newly launched course creator reports not knowing how to obtain testimonials and feeling reluctant to ask for reviews because it could seem pushy.
emails.mechanism: One form, one list. You invite a cohort from Senja individually or in bulk, and you switch on up to three follow-up emails that go out 1, 3 and 7 days after the invite — only to the students who have not responded yet. Set that while you are building the invite, not after it has gone out. Which means the follow-up stops being a weekly judgement call about whether you are nagging your own students and becomes a bound you chose in advance: three, at most, on a fixed schedule, to non-responders only. And on the student's side the thing you are asking for is a personalised page where they leave text or a video — no account to create, nothing to install — which Senja describes as taking about thirty seconds.
emails.belief_shift: Before: getting testimonials out of a cohort means working up the nerve to ask, then deciding every few days whether to nag people who paid me. After: the asking is one form and one invite list, the follow-up is a bound I set once — three emails at most, on a fixed schedule, to non-responders only — and what I am asking a student for is a page with no account and no software, so I can send it this week and stop re-deciding.

Answer it with what is documented and nothing further: the follow-ups are optional, capped at three, sent on a fixed 1/3/7-day schedule, and they only reach students who have not responded — and what is being asked for is a page with no account to create, which Senja describes as about thirty seconds. Do not answer it by claiming students will be glad to get it, or that most of them will answer.

emails.next_step_decision: Whether they are willing to send the ask at all — by seeing exactly how bounded it is before it goes out: who gets invited, how many reminders exist, when they land, and what the student is actually faced with.
emails.next_step_value: A free account lets them build the form, invite a cohort individually or in bulk, switch on up to three follow-ups sent 1, 3 and 7 days after the invite to students who have not responded, and open the student-facing page themselves: text or a video, no account, no software, which Senja describes as about thirty seconds.
emails.next_step_limit: Setting up and sending one invite tells you nothing about what share of a cohort responds, how students feel about the reminders, or whether what arrives is worth putting on a sales page. It also does not cover the automatic, platform-triggered version of the same ask, which needs a paid plan and a connected platform, and it does not settle which plan you would end up on.
emails.subject_strategy: The reader already agrees testimonials matter, so a subject arguing for social proof wastes the open. Name the specific thing they skip — the second ask, the follow-up they never send — in their own plain language, and let the body supply the bounded mechanism. No urgency, no deadline, and no number that could read as a result.

brief.voice_notes: Brand register is direct and mildly irreverent, landing its jokes next to concrete mechanics — keep the irreverence to one line and skip the f-bomb; this is a cold first contact with someone who teaches for a living.
